items.title: Space, Ocean · clue challenge
items.question:
Topics: space, ocean. These words label fictional cards and objects; their pairings do not describe real-world facts.
This is an invented logic grid. Each position contains exactly one value from each group, and each value is used once. Positions run from 1 to 3, left to right. Values in the same position are paired.
Cards: ECLIPSE, NEBULA, OCTOPUS.
Badges: TELESCOPE, REEF, CRATER.
Clues:
1. TELESCOPE is before ECLIPSE.
2. ECLIPSE is before NEBULA.
3. OCTOPUS is next to REEF.
Which value from Badges is paired with OCTOPUS?
items.correctExplanation: The unique complete arrangement gives TELESCOPE. Every stated rule holds.
items.incorrectExplanation: Check the clue combinations. The unique complete arrangement gives TELESCOPE. Every stated rule holds.
items.lessonContent:
Place each group value exactly once.
Translate each clue into positions or pairings.
Combine clues across groups to eliminate impossible arrangements.
Check all clues against the completed table.
Share this: explain which combination of clues fixed the answer.

proofs.scope: the stated fictional groups and rules; complete-grid uniqueness and checked deductions; no human difficulty or enjoyment claim

items.title: Discover the rule
items.question:
An invented machine uses exactly one of these four rules for every input. The labels name observation cards.
Rule A: 1 × input + 7
Rule B: 2 × input + 2
Rule C: 1 × input + 8
Rule D: 3 × input + 4
Examples:
CORAL: input 2 → output 10
GALAXY: input 3 → output 11
CRATER: input 7 → output 15
CURRENT: input 8 → output 16
OCTOPUS: input 12 → output 20
Infer which rule fits every example. What output will it give for input 13?
True or False: the answer is 21.
items.correctExplanation: The claim is true. Only Rule C matches every example. Applying it to 13 gives 21.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 21. Only Rule C matches every example. Applying it to 13 gives 21.
items.lessonContent:
Look for the rule shared by every example.
Test the rule on the next case, rather than guessing from one example.
Reject a rule that fails any stated example.
Check the answer with exact arithmetic or finite enumeration.
Share this: explain which example gave the decisive clue.

proofs.scope: the four displayed candidate rules; unrestricted sequences are not unique

items.title: Space, Ocean · Find the impossible clue
items.question:
Topic labels: space, ocean.
Arrange these cards once each from left to right: TELESCOPE, KELP, COAST, ORBIT, REEF.
Base clues:
TELESCOPE is somewhere to the left of COAST.
REEF is somewhere to the left of KELP.
KELP is somewhere to the left of ORBIT.
COAST is somewhere to the left of REEF.
Test these statements:
Statement A: REEF is somewhere to the left of KELP.
Statement B: COAST is somewhere to the left of REEF.
Statement C: ORBIT is somewhere to the left of COAST.
Statement D: KELP is somewhere to the left of ORBIT.
Which statement is impossible together with the base clues? Answer A, B, C or D.
items.correctExplanation: Statement C contradicts the order forced by the base clues. The other three statements are compatible.
items.incorrectExplanation: Statement C contradicts the order forced by the base clues. The other three statements are compatible.
items.lessonContent:
Connect the stated before-relations into a chain.
Check each candidate statement against the forced order.
One statement must fail while the others remain possible.
Use the contradiction, not a real-world fact about a label.
Share this: identify the chain that made the impossible clue fail.

proofs.scope: only the stated fictional ordering clues

items.title: Cheapest next stop
items.question:
Travel from ORBIT to GALAXY. This invented map has one-way routes; numbers are travel costs. Only listed routes are allowed.
ORBIT → PLANET: 2
ORBIT → REEF: 2
ORBIT → TELESCOPE: 10
ORBIT → GALAXY: 5
PLANET → REEF: 4
REEF → TELESCOPE: 1
TELESCOPE → SALT: 4
SALT → GALAXY: 3
REEF → SALT: 2
Possible first stops: PLANET, REEF, TELESCOPE, GALAXY.
Which first stop minimizes the full trip's cost?
items.correctExplanation: Start with GALAXY. Its cheapest complete trip costs 5, lower than any other first stop's best complete trip.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is GALAXY. Start with GALAXY. Its cheapest complete trip costs 5, lower than any other first stop's best complete trip.
items.lessonContent:
Read every route in its stated direction.
Add the costs along a complete trip to the destination.
Compare the best complete trip through each possible first stop.
A cheap first leg can lead to an expensive full trip.
Share this: explain why the chosen first stop minimizes the total cost.
items.hintText:
Compare the full trip through each possible first stop.
Add every route cost through to the destination; the cheapest first leg need not give the cheapest whole trip.

proofs.scope: the displayed directed routes and positive travel costs

Use the dictionary clue as support, keeping the selected meaning in mind.

items.question:

items.title: Space, Ocean · wonder
items.lessonContent: TELESCOPE has 60,480 distinct letter arrangements, after accounting for repeated letters. OCTOPUS has 2,520 distinct letter arrangements, after accounting for repeated letters. Choosing one arrangement per word gives 152,409,600 combinations: multiply the individual counts. These need not be meaningful words.
items.question:
Topic: space, ocean. For compound entries, spaces and hyphens are omitted.
Take one word from each topic: TELESCOPE, OCTOPUS. Rearrange each word's letters independently, keeping words separate. How many combinations result if you choose one arrangement for each word? How much do repeated letters reduce the number?
